nameStory: The name 'formosa' comes from Latin meaning 'beautiful' or 'lovely,' which perfectly captures this elegant sea slug's appearance. While it lacks a widely-used common name in English, marine biologists often simply call it the 'beautiful doto' in reference to its scientific name.
description: Doto formosa is a tiny sea slug that belongs to a group called nudibranchs - marine snails that have lost their shells and developed external gills instead. These delicate creatures are typically translucent with finger-like projections called cerata extending from their backs. They're quite small, usually measuring less than an inch long, and have a graceful, almost ethereal appearance as they glide across underwater surfaces.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Elongated, translucent body with a distinct head region and finger-like projections (cerata) arranged along the back

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, typically less than an inch in length, requiring close observation or magnification to see details

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Generally translucent to pale with subtle coloring that may appear whitish or slightly yellowish

idTips.label: Cerata arrangement
idTips.description: The finger-like projections extend upward from the back in organized rows, giving a crown-like appearance

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly across surfaces with undulating motion, often appearing to flow like liquid

habitat: Found in New England's cold coastal waters, typically attached to hydroids (small colonial animals) on rocky substrates, dock pilings, and kelp forests. These sea slugs prefer areas with good water circulation in the subtidal zone, usually at depths where recreational divers and snorkelers might encounter them.

seasonality.spring: Most active as water temperatures begin to rise, often found feeding on hydroid colonies that are also becoming more abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when both the sea slugs and their hydroid prey are most numerous and easiest to spot.
seasonality.fall: Still present but may be less active as water temperatures drop and hydroid colonies begin to decline.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed due to cold water temperatures and reduced activity, though some individuals may persist in deeper, more stable waters.

funFact: Doto formosa is essentially a living solar panel - it can incorporate the stinging cells from the hydroids it eats and use them for its own defense, recycling its prey's weapons to protect itself from predators.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small nudibranchs, but the organized arrangement of finger-like cerata in rows along the back is distinctive. Remember: if it looks like a tiny translucent crown gliding underwater, you've likely found a Doto species.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'nudibranch' literally means 'naked gills' - these sea slugs evolved from shelled snails but traded their protective shells for external breathing structures and often brilliant colors or bizarre shapes.
compareHints: Compared to its relative the Crowned Seaslug (Doto coronata), Doto formosa tends to be more translucent and delicate-looking with less pronounced cerata tips. While Doto fragilis is even more fragile-appearing, Doto formosa strikes a middle ground between the robust crowned species and the extremely delicate fragilis form.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Doto species found in New England, the Crowned Seaslug is the most commonly encountered and serves as the 'type species' - essentially the gold standard that defines what a Doto should look like.
Doto fragilis differs from its relative the Crowned Seaslug (Doto coronata) primarily in the shape and arrangement of its cerata - the finger-like projections on its back.
